title: Seeing the Big Picture: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs’ Ability to Interpret and Grade Handwritten Student Work
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can accurately interpret and grade handwritten student mathematics work, and whether their performance differs between routine arithmetic and more complex mathematical illustrations. The authors frame the problem as important for learning analytics and educational assessment because handwritten work is still common in elementary and middle school mathematics, but is expensive for teachers to grade manually.

The study evaluates four MLLMs (Claude 3.5, Claude 3.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and GPT-4.1) in two experiments. Experiment A uses 288 scanned handwritten arithmetic responses from Ghanaian middle school students solving fractions, percentages, and basic algebra problems with objective answers. Experiment B uses 150 student-drawn mathematical illustrations from a DrawEDU subset, drawn from elementary student work in the United States; the models are tested both on the raw images and on the same items augmented with human-written descriptions of the visual content. The design separates visual interpretation from grading by asking models to identify answers and judge correctness under minimal prompting.

The results show that MLLMs can perform near human level on routine handwritten arithmetic, with Gemini 2.5 Pro reaching 95% grading accuracy and 0.90 kappa, but they struggle much more with mathematical illustrations. On image-only illustration tasks, agreement with human judgments is low, and even with human descriptions added performance rises only to moderate agreement levels around 0.43-0.47 kappa, which the authors argue is still insufficient for autonomous deployment. The paper concludes that current MLLMs are promising for grading routine handwritten arithmetic, but they lack the visual and contextual tacit knowledge needed to reliably interpret more ambiguous student mathematical thinking, so human oversight remains necessary for complex cases.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed experimental benchmarking study with a clear comparative design, but it is not an RCT or a classroom efficacy trial. It evaluates model performance on curated datasets rather than measuring learner outcomes, so it meets only limited credibility criteria for causal educational evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows potentially meaningful technical performance for routine arithmetic grading (up to 95% accuracy, LWK=0.90), but this is not direct evidence of student learning gains or deployment impact. For the more realistic illustration task, performance is only moderate and likely insufficient for autonomous use, so overall educational impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: evaluating multimodal LLMs for automated grading and interpretation of handwritten middle school mathematics work, including arithmetic responses and student-drawn mathematical illustrations

finding.finding_summary: On routine handwritten arithmetic with objective answers, the best model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) achieved near-human grading performance: 95% accuracy with linear weighted kappa (LWK) = 0.90 on n=288 middle-school responses from Ghana. Vision accuracy was 89%, suggesting the model could reliably extract and judge standard numerical work under relatively favorable conditions.
finding.measure: Accuracy, precision/recall/F1, linear weighted kappa on grading of handwritten arithmetic responses

finding.finding_summary: For mathematical illustrations from elementary students, direct image-only grading performed substantially worse, with accuracies of 61%-64% and low agreement (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro LWK=0.38; Claude 3.5 LWK=0.23; Claude 3.7 LWK=0.15; GPT-4.1 LWK=0.23) on n=150 items. When given human-written descriptions of the same illustrations, performance improved to 72%-75% accuracy and LWK=0.43-0.47, but still remained below practical deployment thresholds and near the initial human inter-rater ceiling (LWK≈0.45).
finding.measure: Accuracy, linear weighted kappa on grading of student-drawn mathematical illustrations, image-only vs human-description augmented
finding.effect_size: Image-only LWK range=0.15-0.38; human-description LWK range=0.43-0.47

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that automated grading of routine handwritten arithmetic could reduce teacher workload by handling initial scoring and screening. However, it does not report a direct time-savings experiment or teacher-effort effect size; the efficiency claim is inferential from high grading accuracy on n=288 arithmetic responses and the proposed use of MLLMs for human-in-the-loop triage.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / grading automation potential (conceptual, not directly measured)
